title: Knife Throwing: Super Cool
summary: Josh and Chuck explain knife throwing, framing it as an "impalement act" alongside whip cracking, sharpshooting, and archery. They trace the spectacle back to Buffalo Bill's Wild West Shows and discuss the "target girl" tradition and its misogynistic undertones. They cover throwing knife design (weight and balance, dull edges, sharp points, one ounce per inch rule of thumb), the blade throw, handle throw, and no-spin styles (Thorn, Russian, Momun), throwing mechanics and release at the top of the arc, and practice advice. They highlight David Ed Amovitch, the Great Throwdini, whose veiled wheel of death act with two target girls is cited as the most dangerous knife act. The episode also includes ad-style promo banter, a fire alarm intro, and a listener mail segment from Hazel about returning to the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and fire alarm
segments.summary: The hosts open with tour dates and banter about a fire alarm evacuation, fire marshals and orange vest sneak-ins, and Chuck's Peloton workout. Josh plugs his podcast Movie Crush and its Mini Crushes spin-off, and Chuck's guest appearance on it.

segments.title: Introduction to knife throwing and impalement acts
segments.summary: Josh introduces knife throwing as a hobby anyone can learn, with inexpensive throwing knives. He notes the safety warning not to throw kitchen knives or at animals. The hosts describe knife throwing as one of the impalement acts, which also include bullwhip cracking, sharpshooting, and archery.

segments.title: History and Buffalo Bill's Wild West Shows
segments.summary: The hosts trace knife use back thousands of years and say knife throwing spread as a spectacle through Buffalo Bill's Wild West Shows in the United States and Europe. They discuss the target girl tradition and its misogynistic framing.

segments.title: Wheel of death, veiled act, and the Great Throwdini
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Gibsons' wheel of death at Ringling Brothers in Madison Square Garden and other stunts such as balloon-popping and ash-knocking. They describe the veiled wheel of death and the Great Throwdini, David Ed Amovitch, who threw with two target girls on the wheel at about one knife every 0.59 seconds without hitting either.

segments.title: Knife design and choosing throwing knives
segments.summary: The hosts explain that throwing knives should have dull edges and sharp points, and be balanced to throw. They discuss the weight-per-inch rule of thumb and a starter knife of about ten to sixteen ounces and twelve to fourteen inches. Throwing the heavy end first creates spin.

segments.title: Blade throw, handle throw, and distance
segments.summary: The hosts describe the half-turn blade throw, the full-turn handle throw (hatchet or hammer throw), and the double-turn throw. They give approximate distances for each: about seven to eight feet for the half turn, twelve to fifteen for the full turn, and about thirty feet for two turns. They describe stance and the arc of the throw.

segments.title: No-spin styles and practice advice
segments.summary: The hosts cover no-spin throwing styles including Thorn style named after Ralph Thorn, Russian style, and Momun style, and their advantages through tight spaces and reduced joint strain. They advise getting a set of several knives, practicing safely and alone, and not standing near the target.

segments.title: Listener mail from Hazel
segments.summary: The hosts read a listener mail from Hazel, who listened as an eleven-year-old in 2011, stopped at thirteen, and came back to find the show still going. Josh and Chuck mention other social channels and sign off.
